source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head
finding: Founding study. People plan in a small maze with deterministic moves. When a path passes a large loss, they cut the search there, even when that costs them points.
numbers: N=46 healthy volunteers, three groups (15/16/15) differing only in the large loss: -70, -100 or -140 pence. 6 states, 2 buttons, 2-8 move episodes, 24 episodes per block, second block analysed.
quote: it was reflexively evoked by large losses and persisted even when overwhelmingly counterproductive
limits: Healthy, young sample; maze is tiny; pruning is the author-defined model, not directly observed.
agent_relevance: S6 should expect that a branch containing a vivid bad outcome gets cut by default. Tree rules should make pruning a visible, budgeted decision, not a reflex.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head
finding: Model comparison: a look-ahead model with no pruning predicts about 77% of choices; adding discounting, then pruning, then a learned Pavlovian value raises this to about 91%. A habitual SARSA model fits much worse.
numbers: Look-ahead 77% predicted (predictive prob 0.71); best model Pruning and Learned about 91%; goal-directed model beats habit by BIC 314.
limits: Percentages are as extracted from the paper text; some exact statistics were images.
agent_relevance: A depth-limited tree with a separate stop rule after bad outcomes is a better description of search than a full tree.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head
finding: Pruning was specific to the large loss, not general. Specific pruning exceeded general pruning in nearly every subject, and did not shrink when it became costly.
numbers: Specific > general pruning in 14/15 (-70), 12/16 (-100), 14/15 (-140) subjects. No group difference in specific pruning although it was counterproductive in the -70 and -100 groups. Punishments treated as about 1.4 times as aversive as equal rewards.
limits: Pruning cost was zero in the -140 group because an equal path avoided the loss. Loss aversion could explain part of the effect without pruning (authors' caveat).
agent_relevance: Pruning rules must be tied to a check (does the cut branch hold the best answer?) because humans prune on affect, not on value.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head
finding: Pruning model definition: at every tree depth a biased coin stops the search; a separate stop probability applies after large-loss transitions. Binary pruning was used, not graded.
numbers: Four model families: Look-ahead, Discount, Pruning, Pruning and Learned. Separate parameters per group gave no better fit.
limits: Mean-field approximation solves a slightly different decision problem exactly (authors).
agent_relevance: Gives a ready formal template: stop probability per depth plus an extra stop probability on flagged branches.

source: Huys et al. (2012) Bonsai trees in your head
finding: Link to mood: tendency to prune after negative outcomes correlated with mild depressive symptoms; no link to neuroticism. Authors call this a possible vulnerability marker, not proof.
numbers: BDI correlated positively with specific pruning (not general pruning); NEO neuroticism no correlation. Depression judged unlikely in 94%.
limits: Healthy sample, correlational, indirect. Serotonin link untested.
agent_relevance: Pruning is a bias that varies by person and state. Our agent's pruning bias will vary by prompt tone as well; test it.

source: Huys et al. (2015) Interplay of approximate planning strategies
finding: Second study with longer plans (3-5 moves) found people cut the tree into short fragments, solve each greedily, and reuse past fragments. Pruning after large losses still appeared in every subject.
numbers: N=37 analysed of 41. 90 main trials (60 with a large loss on the optimal path). Plans of 3,4,5 moves = 8,16,32 sequences. Pruning remained in 37/37 subjects. Full model explained 78% of variance. Unrestricted fragmentation overfit (iBIC +682 vs baseline).
quote: Subjects exploit the structure of the domain to establish subgoals
limits: One reward structure; reward-driven subgoals may break under other rewards (untested). Fragmentation is inferred, not a process model.
agent_relevance: Hierarchical decomposition and reuse (memoization) are cheaper than deeper pruning alone. Fits S6 depth limits plus reuse of earlier sub-plans.

source: Huys et al. (2015) Interplay of approximate planning strategies
finding: Cost arithmetic: a full depth-3 tree costs about 24 operations; splitting it into a 2-then-1 plan costs 10, a saving of more than half. The inferred splits matched the cheapest split that still picks the optimal first move.
numbers: Cost d x 2^d: 24 vs 10. Depth-1 fragments were preceded by pauses 9.7 ms longer (t(36)=2.17, p=0.037).
limits: The timing effect is tiny. Subgoal sits at state 2 about 90% of the time, partly driven by where the big reward was.
agent_relevance: Budget rule: choose depth by cost d x branching^d and decompose when the full tree exceeds the budget.

source: Huys et al. (2015) Interplay of approximate planning strategies
finding: Stochastic memoization (reusing earlier fragments with a Chinese-restaurant-process rule) improved fit greatly and fragment entropy fell over trials.
numbers: Log-likelihood up 43 +- 22 per subject; 14% more variance; delta iBIC 4162 (86 after controlling reward scaling). Mean fragment length vs verbal IQ rho=0.08, p=0.64.
limits: Memoization independent of reward quality. IQ measure was verbal (WTAR).
agent_relevance: Caching of earlier branch results is a human strategy; the agent can reuse solved sub-branches instead of re-searching.

source: Keramati et al. (2016) Adaptive integration of habits into depth-limited planning
finding: Time pressure makes people plan to a shallower depth and fill in the rest with cached habit values (plan-until-habit). Depth is a covert decision shaped by resources.
numbers: N=30 (15 per group). High-resource limit 2000 ms, low-resource 700 ms per stage. Three-stage task, about 350-500 trials, common/rare transitions P=0.7/0.3. Planning stronger under high resource (rewarded p=0.011, unrewarded p=0.027); plan-until-habit stronger under low resource after rewarded trials (p=0.034).
limits: Small groups (15). Only depths k=0,1,2 distinguishable. Only time pressure tested. The paper is internally inconsistent on trial counts (about 400 vs 350/500).
agent_relevance: S6: depth should be set by the budget, and the leaf value at the cut should be a cheap estimate, not zero.

source: Keramati et al. (2016) Adaptive integration of habits into depth-limited planning
finding: Ruled out: pruning without any leaf value would predict indifference between first choices, and a goal-targeting model would give a habit-like pattern; neither matches the data. Best models mixed full planning with plan-until-habit and no pure habit at stage 1.
numbers: Plan-until-habit weight smaller in high-resource group (permutation p<0.01). Stage-2 habit weights 0.37 +- 0.18 (high) and 0.59 +- 0.23 (low).
limits: Hybrid model fits; k identifiable only in a 3-step task.
agent_relevance: A cut branch needs a substitute value, not silence. Pure pruning to zero is not what people do under time pressure.

source: Keramati, Dezfouli, Piray (2011) Speed/accuracy trade-off between habitual and goal-directed processes
finding: Arbitration model: do tree search only when the value of perfect information about the habit value exceeds the cost of deliberating (reward rate times time). Otherwise use the cached value.
numbers: Simulations only: 40 vs 240 training trials, 3000 runs per condition; deliberation time falls to about zero after about 100 trials in the single-lever task.
quote: an approximately optimal trade-off between speed and accuracy
limits: Simulation, not fits to new data. Assumes perfect model knowledge. Predicts linear (not log) reaction time versus options.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule for when to search at all: expected gain from search vs cost of the tokens. Links to G7 (schema must pay for itself).

source: Sezener, Dezfouli, Keramati (2019) Optimizing the depth and direction of prospective planning using information values
finding: Value of uncertainty resolution (VUR) tells where to expand the tree and when to stop: expand the leaf whose expansion most raises the best strategy value; stop when best VUR is below the cost of one expansion.
numbers: Cost = eps x average reward. Leaf values are normal N(mu, sigma^2); closed-form VUR. Grid world 7x7, gamma=0.95, budget 5-25 expansions; Huys task simulated with 300 runs per condition.
limits: Deterministic transitions only; Gaussian leaf values; myopic one-step expansion (joint choice is NP-complete); qualitative fits only.
agent_relevance: Direct recipe for S6: expand where uncertainty could change the choice, cut where it cannot. Pruning falls out of the rule.

source: Sezener, Dezfouli, Keramati (2019) Optimizing the depth and direction of prospective planning using information values
finding: Pruning of the large-loss branch emerges from the model without a special Pavlovian parameter: a very bad branch has little overlap with the best one, so expanding it has low value. Experienced agents plan shallower as habit values grow certain.
numbers: Simulated punishments -140/-100/-70; depth n in {2,4,6,8,10,12}; model overpredicts optimal choices at depth 2 versus the human data. VUR is inverse-U in gamma (zero at 0 and 1).
limits: Mean-only pruning and variance-only pruning both fail; MCTS/UCT claimed to under-explore. Untested on new human data.
agent_relevance: Pruning on expected benefit, not affect, is the rational version of the human reflex.

source: Snider et al. (2015) Prospective optimization with limited resources
finding: In a fast risky path task, people trade planning depth against how often they replan. Humans behaved like exhaustive search under a fixed work budget.
numbers: N=6 (2 authors). 2x2: speed 63 vs 189 mm/s; penalty -1 vs -50. Depth d about 3.3 (slow) and 2.8 (fast) by path overlap. Brute-force work W_BF=12 +- 2 (fast) and 48 +- 8 (slow) fits better than efficient-algorithm contours (9 +- 1, 21 +- 1). Depth p=1.9e-10, replan period p=1e-7.
quote: humans traded off their depth of computation for the recalculation period
limits: Very small N; depth under-estimated about half by the method; stimuli built to be diagnostic; no neural data.
agent_relevance: Work budget W = (d+1)/r x 2^d sets a trade-off: deeper plans need fewer replans. Use for token budgeting in S6.

source: Snider et al. (2015) Prospective optimization with limited resources
finding: Reaction time: first choice of a trial is slower, slow speed gives longer RT, penalty does not affect RT. RT drops near the end of the stimulus where planned depth exceeds remaining rows.
numbers: Mean RT 991 +- 9 ms; first choice +771 ms; slow +528 ms.
limits: Same small sample.
agent_relevance: Plan once at the start, then replan sparingly; thinking time should be front-loaded.

source: Lally et al. (2017) Neural basis of aversive Pavlovian guidance during planning
finding: Behaviour: the optimal path is found 78% of the time when it avoids a large loss but only 37% when it must pass through one. About 52% of the errors on those trials were aversive pruning.
numbers: N about 37 behavioural (41 recruited). Gap 41 points (t(36)=12.51, p<0.001, d=2.06). Pruning rates per person 4% to 93%. Chance about 11%. Best model Pruning+Loss (iBIC 2466; delta 77.5 over discount-only; gamma_S < gamma_G, t(36)=5.12, d=0.84).
quote: Aversive pruning entails excising from consideration decision tree branches that contain important negative events
limits: Healthy adults, 1.5T scanner, fMRI N 31-35 depending on contrast. Same lab and same recruited sample as Huys 2015 (both report 41 recruited, mean age 23.3), so this is not an independent replication.
agent_relevance: Confirms the pruning effect with a neural measure, but from the same sample as Huys 2015. The reflex is strong and varies a lot between people.

source: Lally et al. (2017) Neural basis of aversive Pavlovian guidance during planning
finding: Neural basis: subgenual cingulate activity tracked the model-based pruning inclination, more strongly on hard trials. Insula responded to receiving large losses and correlated with the pruning index.
numbers: SGC peak (-6,29,-2), t(36)=3.87, pSVC=0.004. Insula r=0.47, p=0.003; DLPFC r=0.35, p=0.034. State anxiety predicted pruning (p=0.042); depression did not.
limits: Timing of pruning inside a trial is unknown, so no causal claim. Too small to split pruners from non-pruners.
agent_relevance: Pruning is a separate process from search itself, so it can be inspected and controlled as its own operator.

source: Mattar & Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay
finding: Planning as choosing which memory backups to run: priority = gain x need. This gives forward and reverse replay and focuses compute near the agent and near rewards.
numbers: Simulated, gamma=0.9, beta=5, 20 planning steps x 50 episodes. Cited data: 841 of 887 forward events before running, 395 of 464 reverse events after running (Diba and Buzsaki).
limits: Gain cannot be computed before the backup; myopic; deterministic; no uncertainty.
agent_relevance: Prioritise expansions by gain (does it change the choice) x need (will we reach it). Same logic as VUR.

source: Newell & Simon / de Groot (cited in literature; not opened)
finding: Classic finding in chess: experts search a similar number of moves to novices but select better ones. Cited in the human planning literature; not checked here.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not opened this session; treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Quality of branch selection may matter more than depth.

source: van Opheusden et al. (2023) Expertise increases planning depth in human gameplay, Nature
finding: Recalled, not read: in a four-in-a-row game a tree-search model with noise, pruning and feature dropping fits humans, and its planning depth rises with expertise.
numbers: Not recorded: page blocked behind a login redirect.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Key forward citation to read next for depth and pruning in expert play.

source: Callaway et al. (2022) Rational use of cognitive resources in human planning, Nature Human Behaviour
finding: Recalled, not read: people choose planning strategies that fit the cost of computation; resource-rational strategies explain how they plan.
numbers: Not recorded: page blocked behind a login redirect.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Read next: resource-rational account of how much to plan.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: Game of 24 with GPT-4: input-output 7.3%, chain-of-thought 4.0%, CoT self-consistency (k=100) 9.0%, tree of thoughts with breadth b=1 45%, b=5 74%.
numbers: 100 games. Best of 100 CoT 49%, best of 100 IO 33%, IO+refine (k=10) 27%. Tree search keeps the best b states per step (BFS, T<=3 steps, b<=5) judged by the model.
limits: One model (GPT-4), one puzzle family; evaluator is the same model (self-judging).
agent_relevance: Shows a breadth-limited tree with pruning beats more independent samples at similar cost. A direct S6 instance.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: Pruning ablation in 5x5 mini crosswords: removing the model-judged pruning hurts; removing backtracking hurts more. But pruning also cut off correct solutions.
numbers: Word-level success: ToT 60%, no prune 41.5%, no backtrack 20%, oracle best state 67.5%; games solved 4/20 vs 7/20 oracle; no-prune found the answer in 4/20 games, 3 of which pruned ToT could not.
quote: Given the state evaluation as a pruning heuristic is imperfect
limits: Pruning heuristic is imperfect (model sometimes called valid words impossible). Output-state choice is a weak point.
agent_relevance: Pruning needs a safety valve: keep a record of pruned branches and revisit when search fails (G6: submit best so far).

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: Cost and generation-vs-evaluation split. ToT on Game of 24 costs about as many tokens as 100 CoT runs but wins. A weaker model as evaluator hurts less than a weaker model as generator.
numbers: ToT 5.5k completion / 1.4k prompt tokens vs CoT best of 100 6.7k/2.2k (49%). Cost-per-case column garbled in extraction; not recorded. GPT-3.5 ToT 19%; GPT-4 generate + GPT-3.5 evaluate 64%; GPT-3.5 generate + GPT-4 evaluate 31%. Creative writing ToT costs about 5x.
limits: Costs from the paper at 2023 prices.
agent_relevance: Spend capable-model tokens on generating candidates; a cheaper judge can prune.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: Blocksworld with LLaMA-33B: chain-of-thought fails on longer plans, search with a world model and MCTS solves most 2- and 4-step problems.
limits: 6-step search space is large; success drops with depth; MCTS iterations (10 vs 20) matter.
agent_relevance: Depth is the weak point. More iterations buy more depth. Budget rule for S6.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search
finding: MCTS-based language agent tree search beats chain-of-thought, ToT and RAP at the same sample complexity on HotPotQA, and reaches state of the art on HumanEval.
numbers: HotpotQA EM (GPT-3.5) reasoning: CoT 0.34, ToT 0.55, RAP 0.60, LATS 0.62; acting: ReAct 0.32, Reflexion 0.51, LATS 0.63 (n=5,k=50), n=10 0.65, CoT+ReAct 0.71. HumanEval pass@1 GPT-4 92.7 vs Reflexion 91.0. WebShop score 75.9.
limits: Uses external environment feedback; value function by the model; costs per node high.
agent_relevance: Tree search beats single-shot only when there is real environment feedback to prune on (matches G2, G3).

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search
finding: Ablation: replacing MCTS with DFS and ToT-style model-judged pruning removes selection and backpropagation and cuts HotPotQA performance by 0.21.
numbers: LATS n=1,k=50: 0.48 vs ReAct best of 250 0.42. Table with k=10: ToT 0.34 (33.97 nodes), RAP 0.44, LATS 0.44 with fewer nodes.
limits: Ablation reported by the authors only; node counts as extracted.
agent_relevance: Pruning by a model score alone is weaker than value statistics gathered across attempts.

source: Lehnert et al. (2024) Beyond A*: Searchformer
finding: Training a transformer on the full trace of A* search (nodes added and removed) then fine-tuning gives a planner that solves Sokoban more often and uses fewer search steps than A*.
numbers: Sokoban: 93.7% optimally solved, up to 26.8% fewer search steps than A*. Maze table: solution-only 90.3 solved/86.8 optimal; search-augmented 92.5/90.8; Searchformer step 3 95.5/93.7. Beats direct-solution models of 5-10x size trained on 10x more data.
limits: Trained model, not scaffold; A* is exact on small grid worlds; trace-length scales with task.
agent_relevance: Writing out the search trace (not just the answer) helps. Related to externalising the tree in the agent's scratchpad.

source: Replication check on Huys 2012 pruning (not an evidence source)
finding: Huys 2015 and Lally 2017 both found pruning after large losses, but they share one recruited sample (41 recruited, mean age 23.3, same lab). No independent-lab replication and no failed replication were found in this pass.
numbers: Not applicable.
limits: Search tools were rate limited, so no forward-citation search was possible this session.
agent_relevance: Open question for angle B: independent replications and LLM tests of Pavlovian-style pruning.
